Game design document · version 1.0

कंचा तोड़

KANCHA TODH

Flick one marble, shatter the rest. A one-thumb arcade game rooted in the Indian street game of kancha, painted in the style of 80s and 90s street art.

Designed and built by Sanidhya Dev Gupta · catsarewhat studios

GenreHyper-casual arcade, physics
PlatformBrowser (WebGL), touch or mouse
EngineUnity 6 (6000.4), URP 2D
TeamOne person, catsarewhat studios
Stage lengthDesigned to stay under a minute
PriceFree, no ads, no sign-up

01Vision

Every Indian childhood has a chalk circle in the dust and a pocket full of kanche. Kancha Todh turns that circle into a tight, replayable arcade game: one marble, one flick, a ring of enemies to break.

Design pillars

1 · Readable, honest flicks

Aim and power are always visible. The player should never wonder what a flick did or why.

2 · One new thing at a time

Each stage adds a single marble, ground or formation, in an otherwise familiar setting.

3 · Loud art, quiet rules

The world is maximalist. The information on top of it is plain, big and on flat banners.

4 · Short runs, long tail

Quick stages, permanent upgrades, and a boss cycle that repeats and tightens.

Audience and session

  • Casual players who play in short, interrupted bursts: commutes, queues, bedtime. One thumb, portrait only, any phone shape.
  • No ads, no purchases, no account. Play stats are off by default and never leave the device.
  • The aim is a stage under a minute. That is a design target; stage length has not been measured with players.

Where the idea came from

The brief was to design a casual game for India, judged on the chain of research, decisions and prototypes as much as on the game. The research (a market scan and ten interviews across four cities) pointed the same way from two directions: sessions are 1 to 3 minutes, frustration ends them at once, and people choose what they already recognise.

Three concepts were explored: a light-propagation puzzle (Jhalar City), a matchbox-art card strategy (Maachiss), and a marble-flicking physics arcade. Kancha mapped most directly onto what the research said.

Design thinking

Why kancha, and not the other two concepts

Problem
A game for short, interrupted sessions with players who quit at the first friction.
Alternatives
A puzzle with voltage and socket rules (needs reading and thinking), and a card strategy (needs setup). Both ask for attention before they give fun.
Deciding constraint
Zero learning cost. Everyone who played kancha already knows the action; the phone only has to make it one-thumb.
Result
The core action is a single gesture, and the design effort could go into clarity and progression instead of teaching.

02Core loop and flows

A stage is a ring of enemy marbles. You flick your own marbles at it, one at a time, until you have broken enough of them or run out.

The stage loop

The moment-to-moment loop: one shot

Run end and restart

The meta loop

Screen flow

The rules, exactly

  • Your queue starts at 6 marbles. It drops to 5 once you have cleared 20 stages and to 4 after 40 (never below 4). On a boss stage you get 2 extra.
  • Each marble has 8 bounces, plus bounces from the Hardness upgrade and some grounds, plus 2 on a boss stage. A bounce is any hit: a wall, an enemy marble or a boss.
  • A stage has a break target. When you reach it, the stage is cleared as soon as your marble in flight ends, or when the ring is empty. It does not end the instant the target is hit, so a good shot can keep scoring.
  • If your queue runs out before the target, the run ends. During a boss fight, an empty queue is a run end.
Design thinking

The stage does not end the moment you hit the target

Problem
Ending a stage mid-shot cuts off the best part of a flick: the chain reaction you just started.
Alternatives
End instantly, or only when the ring is empty.
Decision
Once the target is met the stage waits for the marble in flight to finish, so chains pay out. Clearing the whole ring also ends it.
Design thinking

A failed run still pays

Problem
Short sessions only work if no session feels wasted.
Decision
Shards are banked in full on a cleared stage, and a failed run keeps 30% of the run's shards. Boons reset on a failed run; upgrades never do.
Result
Even a stage 2 failure moves the shop forward, which gives a reason to try once more.

03Controls and feel

Press to aim, hold to charge, release to fire. All with one thumb.

SchemeAimChargeFireCancel
TouchPress anywhere that is not a button. The marble points at your finger; slide to adjust.Keep the finger down.Lift the finger.Slide back onto your own marble (within 0.45 units) and lift.
MousePress the left button anywhere that is not a button.Hold it.Release it.Move back onto your marble and release.
Keyboard, gamepadNot supported. Pause is an on-screen button.

The aim preview

  • Power ring: an ink-outlined ring around the marble. It fills in marigold toward vermilion as power rises.
  • Arrowhead beyond the ring, along the shot.
  • Beads flow along the predicted path: exactly 2 bounces, then a tail of 0.8 units. Enemy marbles are treated as static, so what happens after hitting one is a guide.
  • Ghost rings at each predicted impact, sized like the real marble.
  • Cancel: a grey ring with a cross appears when the finger is on the marble.

Feel values

SystemValue
Power sweep0 to full over 0.9 s, then back, ping-ponging while held
Launch speedBetween 4 (empty) and the launch force (12 by default; 13, 14, 15, 16 or 18 with the Speed upgrade)
Aim coneWithin 80° either side of straight-inward, so you cannot fire into the rim you sit on
Speed after bouncesDecays from launch speed to 50% (never under 4) over the first 5 bounces, then holds
Time in flightA marble breaks after 7 s
Spawn-inA new marble grows in over 0.3 s with an expanding ring
Enemy hit and breakWhite flash for 0.06 s; break pops to 1.4× in 0.07 s, then shrinks away in 0.1 s
Your marble breakingA 0.15 s shake, then a 0.15 s shrink. It darkens as bounces run out.
Screen shakeBoss hit 0.15 over 0.18 s, shield break 0.08 over 0.1 s, decoy pop 0.06 over 0.1 s, Stone Wrestler slam 0.2 over 0.25 s
CritA gold flash for 0.08 s on your marble
Not usedHit-stop, input buffering and aim assist
Design thinking

Redrawing the aim line and power meter

Problem
In the game scene, the aim line and power meter vanished into the ground texture. Players could not tell what a flick would do, which is the one thing they look at on every move.
Alternatives
Trace every bounce (cluttered, and it gives the answer away); trace none (too blind); a bar at the screen edge (too far from the thumb).
Decision
A ring on the marble itself that fills with power, an arrow, and a path of exactly two bounces with ghost rings. Cancel by sliding back onto the marble, so a one-thumb layout needs no extra button.
Result
Aim and power read on every ground. The 80° cone also removed a bug class: firing into the wall you are touching.
Design thinking

Power is timing, not distance

Problem
Drag-back slingshots need room and precision, and fight with a thumb at the bottom of a phone.
Decision
Aim by pointing, set power by when you let go. The ring sweeps every 0.9 s, so the skill is timing, and there is nothing to learn about screen distances.

04World and theme

There is no story. The game is a place: a dusty lane under festival flags, with a chalk circle drawn in the middle of it.

  • Setting: a painted Indian street, in the visual language of truck art, matchbox labels, cinema hoardings, marigold garlands and rangoli.
  • Tone: festive and playful. Nothing is violent; the only things that break are marbles.
  • Marble lore: the six enemy marbles started life with Hindi names (Mitti, Shesha, Peetal, Pathar, Lauh, Jadui: clay, glass, brass, stone, iron, magic). The game shows the English names.
  • Language: all in-game text is English. The only Hindi is the logo, कंचा तोड़, on the main menu.
Design thinking

Cultural rooting is a system, not a skin

Problem
"Make it Indian" can end up as saffron paint on a generic game.
Decision
Build on a real game first, then dress it. The mechanic carries the culture; the art follows it.
Design thinking

English everywhere, Hindi on the logo: a trade-off still open

Problem
Mixed-script labels were small and cluttered at phone size, and Devanagari needed a workaround to render correctly.
Decision
One language, set large, with the logo as the single exception because it is the game's identity.
Tension
The research found regional language to be the access layer for many Indian players. A language option is the first thing to add next. This is an open question, not a closed one.

05Stages

One principle: one new thing per stage, introduced in a familiar setting. Stages 1 to 19 follow a hand-written table. Boss stages are always the Ring on the Tin Sheet. From stage 20 the ground and formation rotate so neighbours never repeat.

The introduction schedule

Formations, as the game places them

These are drawn from the same placement rules the game runs (ring radius 1.8, spacing 0.55 for triangle and square). The arena radius is 3.75.

Stage cards, 1 to 21

Each card shows the formation at that stage's real enemy count. The marble pool shows which marbles can appear (a stage's marble types are drawn at random from this pool by weight).

How a stage is sized

  • Enemy count: min(14, 6 + 2 × stage ÷ 3), rounded down.
  • Break target: the count times a fraction that grows from 0.55 at stage 1 to 0.75 at stage 15, rounded, never below 3 and never above 80% of the count.
  • Enemy HP tier: max(0, (stage + 3) ÷ 7 − 1), so every enemy marble gets +1 HP at stages 11, 18, 25 and so on: a step right after a boss, never on a debut stage.
  • Marble weights: each marble has a base weight (Clay 50, Glass 28, Brass 20, Stone 24, Iron 14, Magic 6). Clay fades by 2 per stage down to 18. A marble gets 2.5× weight on its debut stage and the next one, and at least two copies are guaranteed on the debut stage.
  • The first time a marble, ground, formation or boss appears, a centred card introduces it once.
Design thinking

One new thing at a time

Problem
Difficulty equals churn. Early builds introduced marbles, grounds and shapes in clumps and cycled grounds on a fixed count, which made difficulty spike for no reason the player could see.
Alternatives
A pure formula, or a hand-authored table for everything.
Decision
Hand-author stages 1 to 19 so each new thing meets the player in a setting they already know, then rotate from stage 20. A new marble also gets guaranteed copies and extra spawn weight so it cannot be missed.
Result
The first 19 stages are a readable ramp, and the Info page mirrors the same schedule.
Design thinking

Enemy HP tiers and shrinking queues: answering "too easy"

Problem
Playtesters stacked boons and upgrades and trivialised the game by stage 6.
Decision
Enemy HP gains a tier every seven stages, the break target climbs to 75%, and your queue shrinks from 6 to 5 to 4 as you clear bosses.
Open
This has not been re-tested with players. The Weight upgrade, which takes enemy HP down fast, is the likeliest culprit.

06Enemies and AI

Enemy marbles do not think. They are physics objects that react to hits. Variety comes from weight, toughness and what each one does on impact or when it breaks.

How enemy marbles interact

  • When a moving enemy hits another, it pushes it with speed × mass ratio × 0.7, clamped between 0.5 and 12, scaled by the ground's push multiplier.
  • Then each type adds its own reaction. Stone slows itself to 90% and speeds the marble it hit to 130%. Iron slows the other marble to 60%. Glass speeds the other to 140%. Magic scales the other by a random 0.4 to 2.0.
  • When hit by you, Stone also knocks your marble sideways by 0.4 speed.
  • On break: Glass damages marbles within 1.5 for 1; Brass fires up to 4 marbles within 3 away for 1 damage; Magic has a one in three chance to damage marbles within 2 for 2.
Design thinking

Make physics the AI

Problem
A one-thumb flicking game has no room for enemies that dodge or shoot back: you cannot out-aim something that reacts to you.
Decision
Give enemies mass and a reaction instead of a brain. The player's reading of the table, not reflexes, becomes the skill.
Result
Collisions create the "wait, what just happened?" moments that players named most often in playtests. Bosses are the only enemies with behaviour (next section).

07Bosses

Five bosses at stages 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. After that the cycle repeats from the Glass Queen at stage 60, tougher and 8% faster each lap.

Shared rules

  • Three phases, at 66% and 33% HP. Each phase speeds the boss up (×1.6, then ×2.3), recolours it, spins its shields faster (×2, then ×3.4), and shortens the gap between tricks to 75%, then 55%. Wandering direction changes every 3 s, 2 s, then 1.2 s.
  • Shields absorb one hit each, whatever the damage, in phases 1 and 2. Phase 3 removes them. Hits that land on a shield do not damage the boss.
  • Defeating a boss pays 500 shards and offers a boon.
  • Crits do not apply to bosses.

Boss HP

Bosses 1 to 5 use 50 + 10 × n² where n is the boss number, times a multiplier per boss. After the first five it grows by a flat 70 per boss instead.

A boss's state machine

Design thinking

Five bosses, one trick each, with a tell

Problem
The first boss was a single marble with shields that came back every ten stages with more HP. Players said it felt the same every time.
Alternatives
More HP and more shields; or a different arena for each boss.
Decision
Five bosses, ordered from "only changes how it moves" (dash) to "bends the rules" (decoys). Each trick has a tell the player can read: the Glass Queen flashes and swells, the Stone Wrestler's ring fills, the Magician swells, the Illusionist flashes next to a copy.
Result
Each fight needs a different answer, and the repeat cycle stays beatable because HP grows by a flat 70 instead of quadratically.
Open
Boss difficulty has not been tuned on devices.
Design thinking

A fix that came from a playtest

Problem
Boss shields stayed behind after a retry, orbiting an empty arena. They are children of the arena, not of the boss, so destroying the boss orphaned them.
Decision
Clear shields and summons before the boss is destroyed. The same lesson fixed a slam ring that leaked when a boss was cleared mid-slam.

08Boons

Run-long perks. After each boss you are offered three of the boons you do not have; pick one or skip. They reset when a run ends.

Fire's data value (0.5) is not read by any code; its timing comes from the player and enemy scripts, as described above.

Design thinking

Boons only after bosses

Problem
A small game needs a decision worth talking about, but a choice every stage would break the short loop.
Decision
Offer boons only after a boss, three at a time, one pick or a skip. Playtesters named the boon pick as the most-discussed decision of a run.
Fix from a playtest
Boons used to reset at stage 10 because a stage change called the new-run function. They now reset only on game over, retry or returning to the menu.
Design thinking

Making fire visible

Problem
The fire trail was too small to register as a mechanic, and then it vanished entirely: parented to the marble it never drew, and it collapsed onto the marble while paused.
Decision
A painted flame ribbon, unparented into world space and redrawn from the marble's last positions only while time is running.

09Upgrades and shards

Shards are the soft currency. They buy four permanent upgrades, five levels each, shown as diya lamps.

  • Earning: every enemy marble drops shards when it breaks (see the marble table). A boss pays 500.
  • Banking: a cleared stage banks the run's shards in full. A failed run, or leaving to the menu mid-run, keeps 30% (rounded down).
  • Reset: the shop has a Reset button. It refunds nothing.
Design thinking

Four upgrades, one stat each

Problem
For a one-to-three minute loop to survive a week, it needs progress that carries across runs.
Decision
Four upgrades that each change one thing you can feel: damage, bounces, launch speed, crit. No tree, no currency conversion.
Balance flag
Weight raises damage from 1 to 6, while enemy HP runs 2 to 10 plus a tier every seven stages. It is the strongest upgrade and needs tuning against enemy HP and boss HP.

10Art direction

80s and 90s India: truck art, cinema hoardings, marigold garlands, rangoli. Painted, outlined in deep plum, overflowing with colour. Everything flat that is drawn in code uses the same nine colours.

The palette lives in one place, KTPalette.cs. Painted art in the project was drawn in this family and is left untinted.

Marbles

Grounds

UI frames and HUD pieces

Boons, upgrades and the level lamp

Effects

Where the pieces came from

The project documents the palette, the UI language and how each asset is used. It does not record the tools used to produce the painted art, so this document does not claim one. The art was produced separately and imported as PNG and JPG sheets: backgrounds, framed UI pieces, icon stickers, seamless ground textures, marble textures and effect sheets.

Design thinking

One palette across the whole project

Problem
Colours had drifted screen by screen, so the UI read as several styles.
Decision
A single palette class with named roles. An editor pass snapped existing scene text and flat images to it. Painted art stayed as drawn.
Result
One look everywhere, and one place to change it.
Design thinking

Marbles as sprites, grounds as scrolling worlds

Problem
A marble that rotates with its body reads as a spinning ball. Players read it as "spinning", not "rolling".
Decision
The rolling shader scrolls the texture in world space under the marble instead of rotating with the object, which reads as rolling. Each ground has its own seamless painted fill.

11UI and screens

Also in the game, not shown here: Options, Tutorial (four animated pages), Shop, Pause, Stage clear and Game over.

Screens

  • Main menu: one column of buttons at the same width: PLAY, INFO, OPTIONS, TUTORIAL, then SHOP and QUIT side by side. QUIT is hidden in the browser build.
  • HUD: pause (left), stage plaque with the ground's name (centre), shard counter (right), break progress, your remaining marbles in a pouch, active boon medallions. On boss stages the break bar becomes a boss bar with the boss's name.
  • Info: Marbles (plus bosses), Arenas (plus formations), Game (how to play, boons, upgrades). Anything not yet met shows as a locked silhouette with the stage to reach.
  • Options: music and sound sliders, "Save play stats" (off by default), Clear Data, Replay Tutorial.
  • Tutorial: four animated pages (Aim, Charge, Release, Cancel); opens automatically the first time you press Play.

Type scale

RoleReference size
Titles64
Headings52
Buttons46
Body32
Captions26
Smallest after auto-fit22

Sizes are maximums on a 1080×1920 reference canvas. Text shrinks to fit its box but never below 22. The in-game font is Baloo 2.

Design thinking

Flat banners where painted buttons crowd the words

Problem
Studs and flowers on the painted pill buttons overlapped their labels. The Info page tabs were the worst case.
Alternatives
Narrower label boxes, and cream labels on teal; both helped but did not fix it.
Decision
Painted frames for the big actions and the world; plain banners (ink outline, solid fill, centred label) wherever words need room.
Design thinking

The festive world has to reach the menus

Problem
Playtesters said the UI felt dim next to the world.
Decision
Painted frames, ticket cards, diya pips, confetti, and one palette for the rest.
Design thinking

Marbles spilled out of their pouch

Problem
On a boss stage you get 8 marbles, and the icon row ran past the end of the pouch banner.
Decision
The row now sizes its icons to the space it has, leaving room for the banner's end cap, and tightens the gaps before it shrinks icons further.

12Audio

MusicPlaysFile size
MenuOn the main menu6.7 MB
GameplayFrom the start of every normal stage5.9 MB
BossOn boss stages. It fades out over 1 s when the boss is defeated.5.9 MB

Tempo and key are not recorded in the project. Music fades out over 0.5 s on a game over.

Sound effects

  • Enemy marbles: a hit sound and a break sound for each of the six types.
  • Your marble: launch, bounce, break, crit, spawn.
  • World: arena hit, enemy-on-arena hit, enemy-on-enemy hit.
  • Interface: button click, stage clear, game over, boon select.
  • Boss and boons: boss hit, phase change, shield break, boss defeated, lightning. The fire boon's sound slot is empty.

Volume: music plays at 0.4 and effects at 0.8 of full, each multiplied by the Options slider.

Design thinking

Sound that survives a muted browser tab

Problem
Browsers block audio until the player interacts with the page.
Decision
The itch.io page keeps "click to play" on, so the first click both starts the game and unlocks the sound.

AreaChoiceWhy it matters
EngineUnity 6 (6000.4.0f1), Universal Render Pipeline 2D, legacy Input ManagerOne codebase for browser and Android.
Simulation2D rigid bodies (Box2D). The arena is an edge collider at the rim; your marble uses continuous collision.Collisions are the content, so they are real physics, not scripted patterns.
Aim previewCircle-casts with the marble's real radius, two bounces and a tailWhat the preview shows is what the physics will do, up to the first enemy hit.
Enemy behaviourPer-marble reactions in EnemyMarble; per-boss routines in BossMarbleNo pathfinding or AI tree; boss logic is a handful of timed routines.
DataScriptableObjects for marbles, grounds, boons and upgrades; static catalogues for the stage plan, boss profiles and in-game textRebalancing is an Inspector change.
UIuGUI and TextMeshPro. Info, Options, Tutorial, the stage cards and the menu stack are built from code at runtime.The scenes the author edited by hand are never overwritten by a UI generator.
CameraCameraFitArena keeps the arena and HUD on screen on any aspect ratioOne build fits every phone and window.
SavesPlayerPrefs: shards, upgrade levels, highest stage, tutorial and "seen" flags, volumes, telemetry opt-inSmall, local, no account.
TelemetryJSON lines in a local file, only when the player opts in. Never sent anywhere.Answers where players fail, without a backend.
BuildWebGL (IL2CPP, gzip with the in-browser fallback), 540×960 default canvas, portraitPlays on itch.io.
TestingManual play, plus editor tools to jump to any stage or boss, trigger a boss trick, preview screens and capture frames. There are no automated tests.See the known gaps.
Design thinking

Build new UI at runtime and leave the scenes alone

Problem
The author reworked the HUD by hand because the original was unreadable. The old whole-scene generator would have overwritten that on its next run.
Decision
New screens are drawn from code; the generator is switched off behind a compile flag.
Design thinking

Rolling, not spinning

Problem
The marble texture rotated with the rigid body, so a marble moving in a straight line looked like a spinning ball.
Decision
Overlay UVs use world position instead of object position, so the pattern stays put in the world and appears to roll beneath the marble.
Design thinking

A race that cleared stages twice

Problem
When marbles broke in the same frame, several stage-clear sequences were queued and only one could win.
Decision
A single "clearing" guard flag, and the count of remaining marbles lives in the break function.

14Process and what's next

How it got here

  1. Research. A market scan and ten interviews across four cities, coded into three clusters: ease, mental state, session quality.
  2. Concepts. Three directions explored; kancha chosen.
  3. Six prototype phases, each playable before the next: core arena; launcher and aim; marble types and formations; progression, grounds and the shop; boss and boons; polish and audio.
  4. Informal playtests with friends in five-minute runs. Boss tension and the boon choice landed. Difficulty, clarity and a dim UI did not.
  5. The 1.0 pass. A new aim system, a re-paced stage table, five bosses, Info, Options and Tutorial screens, one palette, larger plain-English type, local opt-in stats, and the painted icons, grounds, marbles and effects.

Known gaps

  • Boss fights and the "too easy" fix have not been tuned or re-tested on devices.
  • The browser build is a large first download (about 90 MB), mostly texture data.
  • The build has been run in a desktop browser only. It has not been run from the itch.io page on iOS or Android.
  • The Android build has not been made yet.
  • The fire boon has no sound.
  • One font, Supply Center, has no licence information in its file and should be confirmed or replaced.
  • The music's source and credits are not recorded in the project.
  • The game is English only.
  • There are no automated tests.

Next

  • Playtest on real phones: aim feel, text sizes, boss difficulty, and the "too easy" finding.
  • Tune shard rewards and upgrade costs against run length, especially Weight.
  • A language option, starting with Hindi.
  • Shrink textures to cut the first download.
  • An Android build.

What the project taught

Research is the spine

The biggest decision, short loops, was made in week one of secondary research.

Physics writes moments

Emergent collisions gave the beats players talked about most.

Feel is half the design

The rolling effect, screen shake and a readable aim line were not in the first spec.

First builds are drafts

Difficulty, boon persistence, clear logic and later the UI language were all rebuilt.
